subject: chemistry
title: The Arrhenius equation
key_idea: The rate constant k rises sharply with temperature, because more collisions have energy of at least Eₐ. The Arrhenius equation, k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT), describes this. A graph of ln k against 1/T is a straight line, and its gradient gives the activation energy.

blocks.text: Rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ changes with temperature only through k. This section covers why k increases with temperature.

items: As temperature rises, the proportion of molecules with energy of at least Eₐ increases (see the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution).
More collisions are effective, so k is larger and the rate is greater.
The relationship is exponential, not linear. A small rise in temperature can make k much larger.
The orders of reaction do not change with temperature.
k increases with temperature.
The effect is exponential.

blocks.text: The Arrhenius equation links k, temperature and activation energy. This section covers its two forms.

items: The temperature must be in kelvin.

The equation and the value of R are given when they are needed.
k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT) shows k rising with T.
ln k = −Eₐ/RT + ln A is a straight line of the form y = mx + c.

sections.heading: Finding activation energy from a graph

blocks.text: Measure k at several temperatures, then plot ln k against 1/T. This section covers the graph and the calculation.

diagram.alt: A straight line sloping downwards: ln k against 1 over T. The line has a negative gradient equal to minus the activation energy divided by R.

items.text: Convert each temperature to kelvin and work out 1/T. Work out ln k for each k.
Plot ln k (y axis) against 1/T (x axis). The points lie on a straight line with a negative gradient.
Calculate the gradient of the line (change in y ÷ change in x).
Eₐ = −gradient × R. Convert to kJ/mol by dividing by 1000.

diagram.alt: A calculation of activation energy from the gradient of an Arrhenius plot, with new numbers each time.
diagram.question: The gradient of a graph of ln k against 1/T is −{g} K. Use R = 8.31 J/K/mol to calculate the activation energy in kJ/mol.

items: Plot ln k against 1/T.
Eₐ = −gradient × R.

checks.q: Explain why the rate constant increases when the temperature increases.
checks.a: A greater proportion of molecules has energy of at least the activation energy. More collisions are effective, so k increases.

checks.q: State the gradient and the intercept of a graph of ln k against 1/T.
The gradient of a graph of ln k against 1/T is −6000 K. Calculate Eₐ in kJ/mol. R = 8.31 J/K/mol.

blocks.text: Know that the pre-exponential factor A is the symbol in the equation. An explanation of A is not required.

items: Determine Eₐ and A graphically from ln k against 1/T.
R is provided on the data sheet, as are the equations.

blocks.text: Use graphical methods to find the activation energy from experimental data.

Plot the graph, draw a line of best fit and find its gradient from a large triangle.

blocks.text: Describe qualitatively the effect of temperature change on the rate constant, and so the rate.

items: State that k increases as temperature increases.
Link this to the greater frequency of effective collisions and a larger proportion of molecules above Eₐ.

blocks.text: Be able to perform calculations using k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT) as well as the graph.

items: Substitute values of A, Eₐ and T into the equation to find k.
Rearrange to find Eₐ or A from values of k at known temperatures. With k₁ at T₁ and k₂ at T₂, subtracting the two logarithmic forms gives ln(k₂ ÷ k₁) = (Eₐ ÷ R) × (1/T₁ − 1/T₂).
The equations and R are given when they are required.
